To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the activation of the gut-brained pathway in response to intraluminal lipid is attenuated in mice prone to develop diet-induced obesity, and that this attenuation may contribute to increased food intake.

1) the number of activated NTS neurons in response to intraluminal lipid is greater in DIO-prone (DIP) than in DIO-resistant (DOR) mice; 2) the activation of NTS is attenuated in DIP mice after 4 and 8 weeks of HF diet; 3) the attenuation of activation of NTS in DIP mice was not associated with changes in the number of Fos+ cells in the dorsal vagal complex
the gut-brain satiation pathway is altered by long term changes to diet.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the neural mechanisms that contribute to the regulation of body weight.
the neural control of food intake and body weight, and our findings suggest that the gut-brain axis may be involved in the development of obesity.
understanding the mechanisms that regulate food intake.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
DIO-P mice exhibit a greater response of hindbrain neurons to intragastrically administered lipid than do DIO-R mice.
diet induced obese-prone (C57Bl/6J) and obese-resistant mice (129sv) differ in the long-term adaptive response of the GI-brain pathway to high-fat diets.
diet-induced obese mice have attenuated gut-brain lipid signaling in response to long-term high fat diet.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
DIO-P mice are more sensitive to high fat diets, and that they have a reduced response to lipid in the gut-brain axis.

DIO-P mice have a decreased response to the lipid signal, and that this decreased response is attenuated further by long term ingestion of a high fat diet, which may contribute in part to the hyperphagia that is seen in this mouse strain.
diet-induced obese mice are less able to respond to satiating signals in the gut, which may be an important contributing factor to increased body weight.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there are differences in how the gut-brain signaling pathway adapts in response to high fat, high calorie diets in mice prone and resistant to obesity.
the gut-brain axis is altered by high fat, energy dense diets, and that the response of the gut to lipid is blunted in obese-prone mice.

the gut-brain signaling pathway in DIO-P and obese-resistant mouse strains is differentially affected by long-term high fat diet, which may be one factor contributing to increased food intake in the obese-prone strain.
